job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Femi Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my two younger sisters. My father runs a small print shop, and I help him with deliveries in the morning and with the machines when they jam. After lunch I walk to the industrial estate and hand my CV to firms in person, because I think a face counts more than a form. On Sundays our family goes to church, and the elders there have been asking around for me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the last stretch of study like, and what are you hoping for next?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied electrical and electronic engineering and passed. My final project was a power-factor correction unit for a workshop, and I built it with my own hands. I had no internship, and about 40 applications, some by post, some at the door, have brought two polite replies and no offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. Machines have always been oversold. A job is a job, and a person who turns up on time and does honest work will be fine. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm still worried. The estate firms say they've no vacancies, and the bigger employers want people with placements. I have debt from my course fees and about two months of savings, and my father keeps saying I'll find something, which makes me feel worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep walking the estate and add the towns nearby by bus, aiming for ten firms a week. I'd ask the church elders, who know some business owners, to put in a word. I'd keep helping in the print shop and take a short course in programmable controllers, about 200 pounds, since factories use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I carry it all day and put on a calm face for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you prefer to go in person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A manager can see I'm serious and I can see the place. Online, my degree is the same as 200 others. I'd rather be remembered as the young man who turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think about the church elders helping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm grateful, and I'm also a bit ashamed. I wanted to get there by myself, but I know that's pride, and that my family needs me to earn.

Ask the church **elders** to put in a word with business owners.
Take a 200-pound **controllers** course and keep helping in the print shop.
feel: **Heavy**; I carry it all day and show a calm face to my family.

fieldNote: Believes in **presence** and honest work over online forms.
Hides his **worry** to protect his family.
Accepts community help from the church elders but feels **shame** about it.

Ask the church elders to speak to business owners
Take a 200-pound programmable controllers course
Keep helping at his father's print shop each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's more noise than substance, but if it's true, then the answer is hard work and learning a skill that matters. I'd say it's wrong for firms to dismiss decent people just to save a few wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one frightens me. Writing, checking and drawing are the junior jobs in engineering, and I've no experience with the tools. I've never used AI, and I don't want to start, but the people who do will be ahead of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go toward the hands-on part of electrical work: installation, testing and maintenance. I'd look for a trade apprenticeship with a local electrician, which pays a little while you learn. I'd tell my father I may have to work under someone for less to start. And I'd pray, quite honestly, and keep asking at the estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, though not in a way anyone sees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to start with AI. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust something that gives answers without showing the work. In my project I did every calculation by hand. If I start, I fear I'll stop thinking for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if an apprenticeship paid very little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it. My family needs me to learn a trade that keeps me working. My mother says honest work is never beneath you, and I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for any family to cope. I'd say our leaders should be honest with people, but I'd not expect the government to carry everyone. Families and churches would have to hold each other up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is the one that scares me. If the thinking side of engineering is done better and cheaper by machines in two years, my degree is a wasted investment, and I have debt. I'd have two months of money and then my father's print shop, which would also suffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take anything with my hands: a labourer on a building site, electrical helper, warehouse. Robots for hands-on work come after, so that's three more years of work. I'd cut all spending but food and transport, and I'd ask the elders for work. I'd help my father with deliveries every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick with worry, yet I'd pray and carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father's print shop have to do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Printing is thinking work too, orders, design, ordering paper. If machines do all that, my father's customers go to a website, and he's sixty. I'd be worrying for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you cope with the debt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paying the minimum and use the rest for the family. If I fell behind, I'd have to talk to the lender, and that would be a shaming day.

say: Two years is too fast for any family to cope, but families and **churches** would hold each other up.
think: If machines do the thinking side of engineering, my degree is a wasted **investment**.
My father's print shop would also **suffer**, and I have debt.

feel: **Sick** with worry, yet I'd pray and carry on.
S2.quote: Printing is thinking work too, orders, design, ordering paper. If machines do all that, my father's customers go to a website, and he's sixty.
fieldNote: His worry covers his **father's** business, not just his own job.
Sees **robots'** delay as three more years of hands-on work.
Fears the **shame** of falling behind on debt.

steps.text: Take building site labouring or electrical helper work
Cut all spending except food and transport
Ask the church elders for any paid work
Work full days at his father's print shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair chance, and sensible people will use it. I'd say apprenticeships and trades should be promoted, because someone has to keep the lights on. I'd tell the young men at church to learn a hands-on skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'm more hopeful. If I get a trade started in the next year, by 2031 I'd have a skill and a licence that machines can't do quickly. It still worries me, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an electrician's apprenticeship and the safety training, and work toward a licence. I'd save 120 a month from wages and the print shop. I'd help my sisters see that a trade is respectable, since my parents want them at university. And I'd pray for the right door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steady. It's easier to carry a worry when it has a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do your parents want your sisters at university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They want a better life than they had. I tell them the world is changing and a degree won't protect anyone. They don't like to hear it from me, since I have one and no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a licence do for you that a degree doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A licence says I can legally do a job, and there's a certificate on the wall. A degree says I studied. Customers want the certificate.

Someone has to keep the **lights** on.

It still worries me, but I can see a **path**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for any family to plan, if they start early. I'd say the young should learn trades and the old should help them, which is how it's always been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still be uneasy but I'd breathe easier. A decade lets me get a first job, build a trade, pay the debt and maybe marry. The danger is that I'd relax and the world would change before I noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first honest job, probably under an electrician, and keep learning. I'd put away 150 a month toward a small house, and I'd save for a wedding. I'd help my father decide whether to keep the print shop or add something that needs hands, like signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Ten years is a long road, but a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you relax too much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting a job and thinking it's safe. The shop my father built was safe until websites took the small jobs. I'd rather stay a little afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not handouts. Fair apprenticeships, lower costs for trade training and a chance for young people to work. I'd rather earn it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I have debt, little money and a father whose shop could be hit too. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a little, trade training I can afford and the church and family staying close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of work. I'm afraid of being useless to my family. If someone gives me a chance, I'll show up every day.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of work. I'm afraid of being useless to my family. If someone gives me a chance, I'll show up every day.
portrait: Femi is a 23-year-old **electrical and electronic engineering** graduate with a pass, no internship and about 40 applications.
He lives with his parents and two sisters, helps in his father's **print shop** and walks the estate handing out his CV.
He is traditional, free-market in outlook, trusts faith and **apprenticeships**, and has never used AI tools.
His mood is **anxious** in gentle worlds and alarmed when the change is fast or the family business is exposed.
He turns to licensed **trade** work, church and family networks and a careful budget.
biggestWorry: The **2028** case, with debt, little savings and his father's shop exposed as well.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships**, affordable trade training and family and church staying close.
